# About This Book

I have been teaching *The Human Brain* for about fifteen years, and other neuroscience courses for a good deal longer. For most of that time this course was built around a website of lecture outlines, which grew steadily more detailed until they had become 28 full chapters — something like 400 pages in all.

That was useful, but it exposed a problem. The material had grown around individual lectures rather than around a coherent account of the brain. Topics appeared wherever a lecture happened to need them, and related ideas ended up separated from one another: the lecture on sleep sat almost entirely apart from the lectures on other forms of hypothalamic control. Conventional textbooks did not fix this. They were organized around a structure I did not want.

The deeper problem was that my own view of how the brain should be taught had changed.

I had become dissatisfied with presenting the brain as a collection of largely separate systems and topics, and I wanted evolution to carry much more of the story. The brain did not appear fully formed as a device for cognition. It emerged within an organism that had to assemble itself, regulate itself, act in the world, compete for resources, avoid danger, reproduce, and anticipate what came next.

I have also come to see control theory as a useful organizing framework. The brain makes more sense to me as part of an embodied control system — one that regulates internal state, selects actions, predicts their consequences, and uses past experience to prepare for uncertain futures — than as an information-processing device. Sleep, in this book, no longer occupies its own compartment; it appears alongside thermoregulation, feeding, and circadian timing, as one more expression of a system regulating an organism against its own anticipated needs.

That perspective made the old lecture structure feel constraining rather than helpful. So I rebuilt the course around a different intellectual arc, and created the textbook that arc required.

## Rebuilding the course

The raw material came from the course itself: the lecture chapters, the slides, and raw transcripts of the lectures. But those materials were only the starting point.

Reorganizing and rewriting them was done over about fifteen months, across a sabbatical semester and two long summers. It required substantial new research, repeated revision, and in many cases rethinking topics I had taught for years. Entire sections were moved, combined, split apart, or rewritten so that ideas introduced in one part of the book could support arguments developed later.

The process was a reminder that teaching a subject for a long time does not mean one's understanding of it stops changing. Revisiting the evidence forced me to update some views, abandon others, and sharpen arguments I had previously treated too casually (and perhaps misunderstood). That was among the most valuable and satisfying parts of the project.

Artificial intelligence tools were used throughout the development of the book for drafting, critique, coding, figure development, and identifying scientific claims that warranted closer examination. I used different systems independently to expose disagreements, weak points, or alternative interpretations in a draft. The organization, conceptual framework, scientific judgments, and final editorial decisions are my own.

## What this book is for

Its immediate purpose is to support the Human Brain course. When lecture chapters are the students' only source, everything has to go into the lectures, because there is nowhere else to send anyone for a fuller account — and the result was a pace that was too compressed and too frenetic.

This book moves the fuller exposition out of the lecture hall. Students can encounter the detailed account here, allowing class time to be spent developing ideas, examining evidence, drawing connections, seeing demonstrations and visualizations, and lingering on the questions that deserve it.

The book is also meant to stand on its own, and it is freely available to anyone who finds the perspective useful. It is written for readers with no previous neuroscience and assumes only the level of biology typically encountered in an introductory university course.

It is a living document. I expect it to keep changing as the science changes, as I teach from it, and as readers reveal places where the explanations, arguments, or organization can be improved. Corrections and objections are welcome, and can be sent to me directly. For students in the Human Brain course, I have set up a thread in Canvas to receive your comments and suggestions.
